title: Entanglement governs early-time growth of randomness in projected ensembles
abstract: Deep thermalization concerns the emergence of universal pure-state statistics in projected ensembles at late times, yet the mechanism governing the initial growth of randomness remains unclear. Here, we study the short-time dynamics of projected ensembles generated from initially unentangled states, quantifying their randomness using frame potentials. For arbitrary Hamiltonians, provided the initial bath state has full support in the measurement basis, we show that the frame potentials to cubic order in time are determined entirely by the subsystem purity, and hence by the bipartite entanglement generated between the unmeasured subsystem and its complement. The entanglement timescale therefore sets the initial timescale for the growth of local randomness, independently of the bath measurement basis. For unitarily invariant Hamiltonian ensembles, we further relate the projected-ensemble frame potential at order $k$ to the $4k$-point spectral form factor, or equivalently to the $2k$th frame potential of the global unitary dynamics, establishing a direct connection between local and global randomness. Our results identify entanglement as the mechanism governing the onset of randomness in projected ensembles and clarify how local randomness emerges from global quantum dynamics.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes how randomness builds up in quantum systems when a subsystem is measured, a process known as projected ensemble dynamics. It proves that the initial rate of this randomness growth is dictated solely by the initial bipartite entanglement between the measured and unmeasured parts of the system. This establishes entanglement as the primary mechanism controlling the onset of local quantum scrambling.
main_problem: The paper investigates the mechanism governing the initial growth of randomness in projected quantum ensembles, contrasting this initial dynamics with the later emergence of universal pure-state statistics (deep thermalization).
main_result: The initial growth of local randomness in projected ensembles is governed entirely by the bipartite entanglement between the unmeasured subsystem and its complement, setting the initial timescale independently of the measurement basis.
method: The analysis quantifies randomness using 'frame potentials' ($F^{(k)}(t)$) and employs time-series expansions (Taylor expansion) to analyze the short-time dynamics of projected states.
model_or_system: The study considers a bipartite quantum system AB, initially in a product state, where subsystem B undergoes measurement, projecting the state onto an ensemble on subsystem A. The dynamics are governed by a general Hamiltonian $H$.
key_observables: Frame potentials ($F^{(k)}(t)$), subsystem purity ($F^{(1)}(t)$), and the entanglement timescale ($	ext{T}_{	ext{ent}}$).
important_parameters: The order of the frame potential ($k$), time ($t$), and the entanglement timescale ($	ext{T}_{	ext{ent}}$).
main_assumptions: The initial bath state must have full support in the measurement basis for the leading-order results to hold; the analysis focuses strictly on the early-time regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate early-time approximations of $F^{(k)}(t)$ for specific models (like the 1D mixed-field Ising model) and compare these results to theoretical predictions derived from spectral form factors.
paper_structure: The paper develops the formalism for frame potentials, derives the early-time expansion for $F^{(k)}(t)$ based on the initial product state, and extends the analysis to unitarily invariant Hamiltonian ensembles, establishing a connection to spectral form factors.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, quantitative link between entanglement measures (bipartite entanglement) and the initial rate of local information scrambling, which is fundamental to understanding thermalization dynamics in many-body quantum systems.
